p: Edmund Burke, the Irish statesman and orator, supported the American colonists in their quarrel with the British Crown and opposed the French revolutionaries with all the force of his genius. His enemies called him inconsistent. He thought himself entirely consistent: the Americans, he said, were defending the ancient liberties of Englishmen against a government that had broken them, while the French were destroying everything old in the name of abstract theories. Whether he was right is a question that every reader of history must decide for himself. I shall try to give you the materials.

By the middle of the eighteenth century, the thirteen British colonies on the eastern coast of North America contained some two million people, prosperous, largely self-governing through their own assemblies, and, until seventeen sixty-three, loyal. In that year Britain ended a long and expensive war with France, which had driven the French out of Canada, and the government in London, burdened with debt, decided that the colonists, who had benefited from the war, should help to pay for their own defence. Parliament passed a series of taxes, the Stamp Act of seventeen sixty-five, upon newspapers and legal documents, and later duties on glass, paper, paint and tea. The colonists objected, not chiefly to the amount, which was small, but to the principle. They were not represented in Parliament, and they held, as Englishmen, that they could be taxed only by their own representatives. No taxation without representation, they said.

The quarrel grew. In December seventeen seventy-three, colonists disguised as Mohawk Indians threw three hundred and forty chests of the East India Company's tea into Boston harbour. Parliament closed the port in punishment. In April seventeen seventy-five, British soldiers marching to seize the colonists' arms at Concord, in Massachusetts, were fired upon at Lexington and Concord, and the war began. On the fourth of July, seventeen seventy-six, the Continental Congress adopted a Declaration of Independence, written chiefly by Thomas Jefferson of Virginia, which declared, in words that have echoed ever since, that all men are created equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable rights, among them life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, and that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed. Jefferson owned some six hundred slaves in the course of his life. The contradiction was noticed at the time, not least by Dr Johnson, who asked how it was that we hear the loudest yelps for liberty among the drivers of negroes.

The war lasted eight years. The Americans, under George Washington, a Virginian planter of no great military brilliance but of immense steadiness and integrity, lost more battles than they won but never lost their army. The decisive help came from France, eager to avenge its defeat by Britain, whose fleet trapped a British army at Yorktown in seventeen eighty-one. By the Treaty of Paris in seventeen eighty-three, Britain recognised the independence of the United States. In seventeen eighty-seven, a convention at Philadelphia drew up a constitution, with a president, a congress and a supreme court, each checking the others, as Montesquieu had recommended; and Washington, having won the war, became its first president, and then, after two terms, went home, which is the rarest of all things in a successful revolutionary.

The French monarchy, having helped the Americans, was bankrupt. By seventeen eighty-eight, interest on its debt consumed half its revenue, and the nobility and clergy, who paid little tax, refused to pay more. King Louis the Sixteenth, a well-meaning, indecisive man, more interested in locksmithing and hunting than in government, summoned the Estates-General, an ancient assembly of the clergy, the nobility and the commons, which had not met since sixteen fourteen. When it met at Versailles in May seventeen eighty-nine, the representatives of the commons, the Third Estate, declared themselves a National Assembly and swore, in a tennis court, not to separate until they had given France a constitution. On the fourteenth of July, the people of Paris stormed the Bastille, a royal fortress and prison, which held at that moment seven prisoners. In August, the Assembly abolished the privileges of the nobility and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen.

For two or three years it seemed that France might become a constitutional monarchy, on something like the English model. It did not. The king tried to flee and was caught. Austria and Prussia threatened war to restore him, and war came in seventeen ninety-two. Under the pressure of war, invasion, food shortage and the fury of the Paris crowd, the Revolution moved to extremes. The monarchy was abolished. The king was tried and guillotined in January seventeen ninety-three, and the queen, Marie Antoinette, in October. A Committee of Public Safety, dominated by Maximilien Robespierre, a lawyer of incorruptible virtue and terrible logic, ruled by what it openly called Terror, and in some eleven months perhaps seventeen thousand people were officially executed and many more died in prison or in the savage repression of revolt in the west of France. Robespierre himself went to the guillotine in July seventeen ninety-four. The Revolution, as one of its victims said, devoured its own children.

After five years of a weak and corrupt government called the Directory, a young general from Corsica, Napoleon Bonaparte, seized power in seventeen ninety-nine and in eighteen hundred and four crowned himself Emperor of the French. He gave France a code of laws, an efficient administration and a centralised state that survive to this day, and he conquered most of Europe before he was destroyed in Russia and finally beaten at Waterloo, in eighteen fifteen, by the Duke of Wellington and the Prussians. My father, who served as a surgeon in that campaign, rarely spoke of it.

The American Revolution produced a republic that has endured, through one terrible civil war, for nearly a century, and which the Encyclopaedia tells me will become the most powerful nation on earth. The French produced terror, dictatorship and twenty years of war, and France has had, since seventeen eighty-nine, two monarchies, two empires, and three republics, the last of which, founded after the defeat of eighteen seventy, is still deciding whether it wishes to exist. Yet the French Revolution had the greater influence on the world. Its ideas, liberty, equality, fraternity, the sovereignty of the nation, the rights of man, the career open to talent, were carried by Napoleon's armies across Europe and could never afterwards be wholly suppressed. Every revolution since, the Encyclopaedia says, has looked back to it, as a model or as a warning. Burke was right that it would end in blood and despotism. He was wrong that its principles would die with it.
